knowledge.text: The general non-desklamp procedure has repeatedly carried temperature-conditioning guidance, and the current edit re-added it to the acquire step: after acquiring the exact target, bring it to the appropriate appliance and perform the explicit "heat X with microwave" or "cool X with fridge" action on the held target as soon as it is admissible, even before opening the appliance; one such action suffices; do not insert/remove the target or toggle the door; then go straight to the destination. In the current pairs where the exact target was located, the Candidate applied the action on the held object at the appliance and avoided the Parent's insertion/door-toggling: in val:0014 (heat tomato to fridge) the Candidate heated the held tomato at the closed microwave (Q4:6) and placed it in 8 steps, while the Parent moved the tomato into the microwave, ran repeated close/open cycles, took it out, and only then heated it for 39 steps (P4:7, P4:36); in val:0015 the Candidate heated the held tomato at the closed microwave (Q5:4) in 7 steps vs the Parent's 8-step open-then-heat (P5:4, P5:5); in val:0011 the Candidate cooled the held plate at the closed fridge (Q1:7) whereas the Parent opened the fridge first (P1:5). The same direct-hold pattern appeared when the guidance was introduced across S1_R03 (cooling a pot at the fridge, heating an apple or egg while holding) and S1_R04 (heating a potato and a tomato while holding), with the Parent instead inserting objects and cycling doors.

This temperature guidance is conditional on locating the exact target and gave no observed benefit when the target was not found: in val:0013 (heat apple to diningtable) both the Parent and the Candidate searched cabinets, countertops, drawers and the fridge, never located an apple, and hit the 50-step limit without performing any temperature action (P3:50, Q3:50). The same limit appears in the earlier history: in a heat-plate pair the Parent found the plate on a countertop and succeeded in 13 steps while the Candidate never reached that countertop and hit the step limit (S1_R04/P2:13, S1_R04/Q2:50), and in a hot-mug pair the exact mug was not found, the Parent took and heated a cup substitute (S1_R04/P1:28, S1_R04/P1:31) while the Candidate kept searching cabinets and hit the limit without success (S1_R04/Q1:50). These instances mark cases where the clause's triggering condition (the exact target in hand at the appliance) was never reached, not evidence that the clause is ineffective.

The current edit refined the general single-pass sweep by treating each individual closed container (cabinet, drawer, fridge, microwave, safe, etc.) and each open surface as a separate candidate, not concluding a container family from one or two empty members, leaving immediately from an already-open empty or redundant receptacle, and abandoning a small set of locations that keeps reappearing without yielding the target. A coverage rescue accompanied it: in val:0016 (put two book in desk) the Parent's 50 recorded steps contain no visit to bed 1 and it hit the step limit cycling among the desk, drawers 1-4 and shelves 1-2, whereas the Candidate expanded to bed 1, took book 1, placed it in the desk, returned to bed 1 for book 2, and completed in 40 steps (Q6:33, Q6:34, Q6:38, Q6:40). In val:0012 (put a cool tomato in microwave) the Candidate reached countertop 2 and finished in 10 steps vs the Parent's 18 steps of cycling among the fridge, cabinet 1, countertop 1 and toaster before reaching countertop 2 (P2:12, Q2:4). Across the seven current pairs the Parent succeeded 5/7 and the Candidate 6/7, the difference being this val:0016 two-book rescue (each task run once). Broader per-candidate coverage can also add steps when the target is found elsewhere quickly: in val:0011 the Candidate inspected an extra empty cabinet 1 before finding the plate on countertop 2 and finished in 9 steps vs the Parent's 8 (Q1:1, Q1:2, Q1:5, P1:8).

The refinement did not overcome step-limit cycling when the target could not be found: in val:0013 (heat apple to diningtable) both the Parent and the Candidate cycled among the same cabinets, countertops, fridge and drawers and hit the 50-step limit without locating an apple (P3:30, P3:50, Q3:30, Q3:50), so the "leave immediately / stop revisiting, continue to new candidates" language did not break the loop within the budget; its benefit stayed conditional on the exact target being present at a location the sweep reaches.

The earlier single-pass family-sweep rewrite (S1_R05) was associated with two rescues where the exact target lay in a family the Parent never reached - put-a-clean-butterknife-in-drawer (the Parent hit the step limit without checking countertop2, while the Candidate found the exact butterknife there, cleaned it at the sinkbasin and placed it in drawer1) and put-a-clean-soapbar-in-cabinet (the Parent cycled among cabinets, sinkbasin and countertop without checking shelf1, while the Candidate found the exact soapbar on shelf1, cleaned it and placed it in cabinet1) - but it did not reliably prevent cycling: in a clean-butterknife pair with no exact butterknife present both executions hit the step limit (the Parent took a knife substitute and the Candidate cycled among drawers, countertops and cabinets), and in a cool-apple pair both succeeded but the Candidate required more steps (46 vs 38). Across those ten paired tasks the Parent succeeded 7/10 and the Candidate 9/10, one trial each, and the two rescues depended on the target being present in an uninspected family; the sweep is not shown to overcome step-limit cycling when the target is absent or unlocated within the budget.
